doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Richardson quartet at the Cable Car Village; Jerome leaves with Hines
summary: The quartet plays opposite the Ink Spots and backs Ella Mae Morse; Richardson abruptly leaves, and his oboe study is noted.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: They had a memorial for him in New York and they had one here. And who should show up? Jackie Kelson showed up. The Basie band was laying over preparatory to going to Japan. So Jack Kelson, he came in, and Jerry Dodgion, he was in town with that band from New York, Carnegie Hall.

They were doing Concord so he played at Jerome’s memorial. But getting back to this quartet, so we played the Village and then we came over here to San Francisco and we played, that was the Diamond Knee with Krupa. I was with the Jerome Richardson Quartet. And then we played at a place called the Cable Car Village, that’s just at the foot of Nob Hill on California Street. And so we played opposite, they were bringing in different groups so we played opposite the Ink Spots.
Oh yeah. Oh what a good gig. And then they brought in Ella Mae Morse, and we backed her, and she loved the band. Because I knew all of her records, all of her records.
That’s so great, when you’re listening to those records.

“Cow Cow Boogie.” Oh yeah. And then from there we went to the Champagne Supper Club down in the Western Addition. And so Hines came through, Jerome didn’t tell me but Hines came through at the Hangover and his saxophone — when he left, Jerome left with him. And so I went to work the second week on the Champagne Supper Club and there was another band on the bandstand. Jerome had split town. And he hadn’t told anybody. So anyhow that was my experience with the Jerome Richardson Quartet. It was a good quartet too. Jerome arranged, he did the arranging and the singing. He was extremely talented. And he played like the oddball horns, he played bassoon, oboe, English horn. Yeah he learned them all at the State Teacher’s College.

Because in our Navy band he played the oboe. And he taught this other, Jimmy Shorter that I mentioned, the pianist from Washington, D.C., he taught him how to play the bassoon. A double reed instrument.
